about: The expert council, item 8, part 3 (queue expert-council): spaced learning. Professors of learning science agree on what makes knowledge last: recall it from memory instead of re-reading it, space the recalls over growing gaps, mix subjects, and explain it to someone else. Most people read once and forget. This is the small system that keeps what a person learns: one thing worth keeping, recalled on a rhythm, for a few minutes a day. Paraphrased from common practice; content only, the screen is not built yet.

loop.cue: After reading, a course or a mistake: 'What is the one thing worth keeping?' Each morning: the day's few recalls on Today.
loop.smallestStep: One recall: read the question, answer in your head, tap whether you knew it. Under a minute.
loop.reward: A card that survives five recalls is marked Kept; the count of things kept this year grows.
loop.environment: Capture is one tap from the Inbox and the share sheet; recalls sit beside the morning routine, never in a separate app.
loop.review: Monthly: retire cards that no longer matter; turn one kept card into something used (a change at work, a note shared).
loop.constraint: Too many cards. One new card a day at most; a daily recall list longer than ten is cut to the ten most overdue.

principles.text: Pulling an answer out of memory strengthens it far more than reading it again.
Recall just as you are about to forget; each success earns a longer gap.
Mix subjects in one sitting; it feels harder and lasts longer.
Tie the new idea to something you already know, and to a real case of your own.
If you cannot explain it simply to someone else, you do not know it yet.
Knowledge used within a week stays; knowledge only stored fades.

fields.ask: A question your future self should be able to answer.
The answer in your own words, two lines at most.
Why it matters to you: one real situation where you will use it.
Where it came from (a title is enough).

good: Your words, not a copied passage.
Prefer why and how over what.
starters: What would I do differently next time because of this?
What is the rule, and when does it not apply?
How would I explain this to a twelve-year-old?

schedule.say: Gaps in days after each successful recall. A miss goes back to the start, kindly; it is how the method works, not a failure.

rituals.do: The day's recalls, answer first, then check.
Explain one kept idea to a person, or write it as five plain sentences.
Pick one idea and change one thing at work or at home because of it.
A mistake becomes a card the same day: what happened, and what to do instead.

plans.name: A book
plans.do: Three cards per book, written after closing it, from memory.

plans.name: A course or certification
plans.do: One card per lesson; a practice paper in place of re-reading; the exam date in the calendar and the gaps planned back from it.

plans.name: A skill (a language, an instrument, a tool)
plans.do: Practice at the edge of what you can do, 20 minutes, with feedback; cards only for the rules.

plans.name: Lessons from work
plans.do: One card from each review, incident or piece of feedback.

plans.name: Helping a child study
plans.do: Ask them to teach you the lesson; quiz on yesterday and last week before today's chapter.

persona.who: A professional preparing for a certification
A reader who forgets every book
A parent of a school child
